Lecture 16 · Part 1Panoramic Image Formation

Lecturer: Prof Andrew Flatau, BDS (Hons 1), BA (Hons 1), PhD, FPFA, FICD — Centre for Rural Dentistry & Oral Health. Main source: White and Pharoah, Oral Radiology (2014).

  • Panoramic radiography is a curved-plane tomographic technique. One image shows both jaws, the teeth and the supporting structures. (standard texts)
  • The X-ray source and the image receptor move around the patient in opposite directions, about moving centres of rotation.
  • Collimators: metallic barriers with a central circular or rectangular aperture. They reduce the size of the beam, the area of tissue irradiated and the number of scattered photons reaching the receptor.
  • A secondary rectangular slit collimator sits in front of the image receptor.
  • The beam is aimed slightly upward, a negative vertical angle. This is why ghost images sit higher than the real object (see Part 5).

The focal trough

  • Focal trough (image layer): the 3-D curved zone in which structures are reasonably sharp on the image.
  • The closer a structure lies to the centre of the trough, the sharper its image.
  • The trough is narrow anteriorly and wide posteriorly, so the incisor region is the most sensitive to positioning errors. (standard texts)
  • Structures outside the trough are blurred and magnified or minified (see Part 6).

Lecture 16 · Part 3Hard Palate and Nasal Floor

Two horizontal radiopaque lines cross the maxilla above the root apices. Texts disagree on what each line represents.

SourceSuperior line (red, more diffuse)Inferior line (blue)
White and Pharoah, 7th ed. (2014)Junction of the nasal septum and nasal fossa floor on the tube side (a ghost image from the opposite side)Junction of the lateral wall of the nasal cavity and the hard palate (nasal floor) on the receptor side (real image)
White and Pharoah, 6th ed.The opposite interpretation
Damante et al. (1998)Junction of the nasal septum and nasal fossa floor. Several superior lines may be projections of anterior hard tissues from the vertical beam angle or head tilt.The nasal fossa floor, especially its lateral and anterior borders
Prof Bill Skarfe—The hard palate
  • Tube side = the side of the X-ray source, which produces the diffuse ghost images. It is the side opposite the real image on the receptor side.
Spelling on slide 8: the slide reads "Demante". The author in the bibliography is Damante JH (Oral Surg Oral Med Oral Pathol 1998; 85: 479–484).

Air spacePosition

Positioning point: the patient presses the tongue against the palate during exposure. This removes the palatoglossal air space from over the maxillary apices. (standard texts)

Lecture 16 · Part 5Real, Double and Ghost Images

Image typeHow it formsAppearanceExamples
Real imageObject within the focal trough, on the receptor sideSharp; on its own sideTeeth, jaws
Double imageObject lies between the X-ray tube and the receptor twice, at the same distance from the receptor both times. This generally means a structure in or close to the midline.Two images, one on each sideCervical spine, hyoid bone (slide); epiglottis, hard palate (standard texts)
Ghost imageDense object outside the focal plane that attenuates the beam enough to project an imageOn the opposite side; blurred; magnified; higher than the real image, because the tube is angled upwardEarrings, contralateral mandible, cervical spine

The spine shadow

  • The cervical spine can produce a radiopaque ghost over the anterior mandible, reducing detail in the incisor region.
  • It is worse when the patient slumps. Correction: patient stands or sits upright with the neck extended. (standard texts)
Two labels for one structure: slide 5 lists the cervical spine as a double image; slide 20 shows it as a ghost shadow. Both occur. As a midline structure it can be imaged twice (double); as a dense structure outside the focal plane it also projects a ghost.

Jewellery artefacts

  • Remove earrings, other jewellery, glasses, hairpins and removable prostheses before exposure. (standard texts)

Lecture 16 · Part 6Distortion and Positioning Errors

Position relative to the focal trough

Object positionResult
Centre of the focal troughMinimal distortion
5 mm posterior to the troughHorizontal magnification of the ring and the mandibular teeth (teeth look wide)
5 mm anterior to the troughHorizontal minification of the ring and the mandibular teeth (teeth look narrow)

Rotation of the head

The side to which the head is rotated is:

  • further from the image receptor and further from the spine
  • magnified horizontally (molars, ramus and condyle look wider)
  • subject to more overlap of the molar images; the greater the rotation, the greater the overlap

Chin position

  • Correct position: the alar–tragal line (tragus of the ear to the ala of the nose) is horizontal.
  • The commonest head-positioning error is the position of the chin.
ErrorAppearance on the slidesAdditional signs (standard texts)
Chin too low (tipped down)Exaggerated "smile" curve; incisors blurredLower incisor apices out of the trough; condyles may be cut off the top of the image
Chin too high (tipped up)Condyles splayed; incisors blurredFlat or reversed ("frown") occlusal plane; hard palate shadow over the maxillary root apices

Patient too far back—Anterior teeth wide and blurred (posterior to the trough)

Paralleling techniqueBisecting-angle technique

Lecture 16 · Part 8Normal Anatomy on Periapicals

Lamina dura and periodontal ligament space

  • Lamina dura ("hard layer"): a thin radiopaque layer of bone lining the tooth socket.
  • It is a developmental extension of the lining of the bony crypt of the tooth germ.
  • Its image comes from the X-ray beam passing tangentially through it: the "egg-shell effect". The more oblique the beam, the more diffuse the lamina dura.
  • PDL space: the thin radiolucent band between the root surface and the lamina dura. (standard texts)
  • A double PDL space and lamina dura may be seen where the proximal root surface is convex.
  • The lamina dura can be hard to see around a healthy tooth and may be clearer on one surface than another. A faint lamina dura on its own is not a sign of disease.

Nutrient canals and the mandibular canal

  • Nutrient canals are normal and usually of fairly uniform width.
  • They run vertically from the inferior dental canal to the apical foramen of a tooth, or to an interdental point of entry to the periodontium.
  • They appear on periapicals in both normal and diseased jaws.
  • A bifid mandibular canal has a second, usually narrower, canal. Reference: Miličević et al., Acta Stomatol Croat 2021; 55(3): 248–255.

Trabecular pattern

RegionTrabecular pattern
Posterior mandibleVariable; large marrow spaces and sparse trabeculation, especially inferiorly
Anterior mandibleCoarser trabecular plates and larger marrow spaces than the anterior maxilla
Anterior maxillaFine trabeculae with many small marrow spaces

Nasal floor and maxillary sinus

  • The floor of the nasal aperture is often seen above the maxillary incisor and canine on periapicals.
  • The anterior border of the maxillary sinus crosses the floor of the nasal fossa in the canine region. Together they form the inverted Y. (standard texts)
  • After tooth loss the sinus floor can extend toward the alveolar crest (pneumatisation).
  • On every panoramic and periapical image, assess the relationship of the maxillary sinus to the maxillary teeth: extraction risk, alveolar resorption and symptoms.
  • Revise with this topic: the superior alveolar nerves, the variable shape of the maxillary sinus, and its bony septa.
